$comment: The plot palette. Single source of truth for both projects.
Edit THIS file, then run tools/gen-palette.mjs, which regenerates
plot-web/shared/src/palette.ts and the Kotlin PlotPalette.kt. Neither
generated file should be edited by hand.
A plot's colour_index (0-7) is assigned by fieldar.pick_colour_index() so
that no two plots within 500 m share a slot. Colours are chosen to survive
the two backgrounds this app actually runs against: satellite imagery of
farmland, and a phone camera pointed at a field. Both are dominated by
green and brown, so there is no green in the palette - a green boundary on
a green crop is the one combination guaranteed to disappear. White is
included because the first field test happened after dark, where it reads
better than any hue.

alpha.$comment: Opacity each surface is drawn at, so the web tool and the AR overlay agree. wallFill is low because walls overlap: standing inside a plot puts four of them in frame at once, and anything heavier compounds into solid colour.

$comment: Crop-health severity ramp, shared by the web map and the AR overlay.
Kept apart from the plot palette above on purpose: that palette answers
'which plot is this', this one answers 'how is the crop doing'. Reusing one
for the other would make a red-slot plot look like a dying plot.
The bad end is brown rather than red because brown is what failed ground
actually looks like, so the grading reads as a description rather than an
alarm - and red is already spoken for by plot slot 0.
fillAlpha rises with severity. Healthy cells are context and must not paint
over the crop the agent came to look at; a critical patch is the answer to
the question and is allowed to be assertive. A single flat alpha made a
whole plot look uniformly tinted, which is the opposite of the point.
